From refugees to sommeliers and wine makers

By: Annalise Lubbe | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
They arrived from Zimbabwe as refugees, in search of a better life, but their journey took them on an unexpected road of discovery and a taste of wine that put them on the map.

Unique Selling Point:
This is a story of two non-drinkers from Zimbabwe ending up as award winning sommeliers and wine makers in the Cape after fleeing the country during economic meltdown 14 years ago. Tinashe Nyamudoka and Joseph Dhafana have worked their way up from menial jobs to earn a living and today they are respected sommeliers who have taken their passion for wine to the next level of wine producing their own brand.

Summary:
In 2007 economic hardships hit Zimbabwe. Prices were doubling every 24 hours and a monthly wage would not even cover your bus fare. By 2008 roughly 1.5 million Zimbabwens were in South Africa. Among the growing numbers of Zimbabweans were Joseph Dhafana and Tinashe Nyamudoka who escaped poverty in search of a better life.

Along their perilous journey they discovered a taste for wine which changed their lives from impoverished refugees to becoming leading sommeliers in the Western Cape and entering the global arena of wine tasting. Ten years after arriving in South Africa Dhafana and Nyamudoka, competed in the World Blind Wine Tasting Championship in Burgundy, France where some of the world’s top wines have to be identified in a blind tasting. Despite very little experience of international and local wines they came in 14th position in 2018 when they competed again. But their story did not end there. Since then they both tried their hand at wine making and took their brand to the international market: Nyamudoka with Mosi wines and Dhafana with Kumusha wines.

Our story will track their stories and the exceptional talent they have for wine and what it took to succeed.


Further information:
Joseph Dhafana:
Joseph Dhafana and his wife Amelia arrived in South Africa in 2009. Despite many challenges including refugee camps and living in a Methodist Church in Johannesburg whilst awaiting asylum, they finally boarded a train from Johannesburg to Cape Town and found themselves in Riebeek Kasteel where Joseph started working as a gardener. Joseph joined Bar Bar Black Sheep restaurant as a dish washer and worked his way up through the kitchen, into the bar and onto the floor as a waiter. On his 29th birthday he tasted his first glass of wine, a Pieter Cruythoff Methode Cap Classique. Joseph remembered his initial sip of wine way back then was a bitter, acidic burn taste but was soon converted. Joseph recalls that with his mind in the vineyards, he pondered how someone could convert grapes to such a wonderful liquid. The wine bug followed him from that day.

In 2013 Joseph enrolled at the Cape Wine Academy. He eventually left Riebeek Kasteel to further pursue his new-found passion in Cape Town and in 2014 got his first opportunity to produce his own wine at Antebellum Wines based at Meerhof Cellars. His meteoric rise to one of the most recognisable young figures in the wine industry is nothing short of remarkable. He worked at the internationally acclaimed La Colombe restaurant in Constantia as head sommelier, became a board member of the Black Cellar Club and was selected to represent South Africa in the World Blind Wine Tasting Championship in Burgundy in 2016 and the following two years as Zim team leader.

In 2019 he left La Colombe to focus on his own wine label, Mosi wines and spirits, a tribute to his Zimbabwean origins and his family. Victoria Falls, known locally as Mosi-oa-tunya, are the face of the Mosi wine label. Joseph currently produces Tinashe Chenin Blanc which was named after his son and flavian Syrah, named after his dad who passed on in 2004. Joseph also produces gin and hopes to add Vodka to the mix in the near future.

Tinashe Nyamudoka
In 2009 Zimbabwe was going into an economic meltdown. At the time Tinash Myamudoka worked at a supermarket and experienced first-hand empty shelves. This prompted his move to South Africa where he found work polishing cutlery at a fine dining restaurant, The Roundhouse. After being promoted to waiter and without any prior experience of wine, Tinash learned from the beverage director, eventually landina job as a wine steward at Nobu - an establishment of the One & Only group.

In 2013 he won the Reaching for the Young Stars Best wine Steward Award. He then worked at the Oyster Box hotel in Durban, before returning to Cape Town to become the head sommelier at The Test Kitchen. Under the guidance of award winning chef and owner of the restaurant Tinashe hones his skills at one of the world’s top 50 best restaurants under the guidance of Dale Luke Robert, head chef and owner. He wins the Eat Out Wine Service Award and with a head for business he completed his diploma from the Cape Wine academy, a Certificate from the Court Master Sommeliers Europe, A certificate in Wine Business Management from the University of Cape Town’s Graduate School of Business and a Michael Fridjhon Wine Judging Academy certificate.

By now Tinashe had extended his wine tasting experience as a top sommelier and felt the time was ripe to try his hand at winemaking. With his roots still firmly entrenched in Zimbabwe he called his brand, Kumusha, meaning ‘your roots’, ‘your home’, ‘your origin’. The challenge he faced when studying wines was associating it with European fruits such as black currents and quince. He always yearned to connect it to indigenous flavours and aromas that resonated with on and ther spaces,hence Kumusha Wines flavours are wild fruits he grew up eating at home. For example, he used the leaf of a black jack (‘Knapse Kerels') - a typical weed that sticks to your clothes - to replace the traditional Black Currant leaf flavour.

In 2020 Tinashe leaves his position as sommelier at the Test Kitchen to focus entirely on Kumusha wines which are now exported to USA, Zimbabwe, Kenya and the Netherlands and can now add the UK after a recent visit to break into this difficult market.

Fast forward to March 2022 and Tinashe is back at the Test Kitchen! This time a brand new restaurant in Johannesburg where Dale Luke Roberts have designed the ultimate culinary experience in a 12 course menu complimented by a carefully selected wine list put together by Tinashe.

Ask what the future holds for Tinashe and he already has his eyes set on making his own brandy to add to his wine making skills and hope to one day go grow wine on his grandfather’s farm in Zimbabwe.

The story:
Our story starts in a very busy Test Kitchen restaurant where the action and pace is fast. Tinashe goes through the wine selection, the chef prepares designer meals and the clock is ticking. From here we will go back to the past of where Tinashe started when he came to South Africa as a migrant and ending up as a top sommelier and wine maker. Joseph’s story will be captured at the tin shack where he lived for a while in Riebeek Kasteel when he was working as a gardner at the Bar Bar Black Sheep restaurant in Riebeek Kasteel up to his winemaking at the local co-op where Mosi wines are bottled.
Interviews will be with Joseph and Tinashe and a short interview with Dale Luke Roberts who can talk about the importance of wine pairing and having a top sommelier on your dining room floor.

Script:


FINAL Script: From refugees to sommeliers and wine makers
DURATION: 9 MINUTES
Date: 8 April 2022


V/O This is a story about wine…..at least, in part. It’s also a story about two refugees. About desperation, perseverance and - ultimately - triumph. To tell it, we must start in Zimbabwe.

Music up - change of pace

V/O In 2009 Zimbabwe was on the brink: political turmoil and economic hardship saw anger spilling into the streets with a predictable and ofen ruthless response from the government. Hunger was widespread.

Joseph Dhafana: Sommelier and wine maker: It was quite clear to all that that short period of time Zim was going through a crisis in terms of there was no food on the shelves. So there came really a time whereby I realise it is really pointless to be stuck in Zim.

V/O Then 28 and working at a cement factory, Joseph Dhafana faced a stark choice: live with growing uncertainty or flee. Like thousands of others, he crossed into South Africa with just the clothes on his back.

Joseph Dhafana: So I arrived in Musina and then I went straight to the refugee camp. Then I stayed there for almost two weeks until I was granted asylum which was to work and study in South Africa.

Claire Mawisa: When you came to SA did you have a plan, did you have a job?

Joseph Dhafana: I came down to Joburg and I lived in a Methodist church. So that time ladies could sleep in the church and gents in the streets. So I slept in the city of Joburg for about two weeks.

Claire Mawisa: Where were you getting food? From bins, handouts?

Joseph Dhafana: Foodwise I could actually get food from the streets and I could wait until I am super hungry then I would just eat without even looking what was on my plate.

V/O It’s a struggle Tinashe Nyamudoka knows too well. Like Joseph, he had a job but chose to leave when he saw the writing on the wall.

Tinashe Nyamudoka: Sommelier and wine maker: I was working in a supermarket, I was actually a junior manager and I saw first hand how the shelves were empty you know. You had money but you didn’t have anything to buy with it.

V/O Tinashe made his way to Cape Town where he hoped to work in a supermarket.

Tinashe Nyamudoka: Obviously you realise you don’t have the documentation required, second of all there weren’t positions for black people like me in those supermarkets so that was a bit of a reality check that sometimes the grass seems greener across but it was really tough.

V/O He eventually got a job in a bakery and then in a restaurant.

Claire Mawisa: So you say you got into restaurants. What were you doing in your first restaurant gig here in South Africa?

Tinashe Nyamudoka: I just got employed because they were looking for inexperienced people.

V/O Joseph’s search for work was more difficult. After weeks on Joh’burg’s streets he made his way to the Western Cape, settling in the wineland’s town of Riebeek Kasteel, where he lived in this shack. It was a move that would dramatically change his fortunes.

Link: This is where Joseph first started working in Riebeek Kasteel as a gardener on this property but it didn’t take him long to move to a restaurant where he first worked as a barman, then a waiter.

Joseph Dhafana: Now you have to understand Joseph is a rural boy, Joseph doesn’t even know a single easy cocktail. I don’t come from a background where wine was made. Wine wasn’t a thing.

V/O His parents were strict Pentacostal Christians who frowned on alcohol. As a 29-year-old Joseph was to have his first taste.

Joseph Dhafana: So 2010, still as a barman that is where I tried my very first sip of wine.

Claire Mawisa; and how was it?

Joseph Dhafana: And I didn’t like it.

Claire Mawisa: (laughs)

Joseph Dhafana: (smiles)

V/O But not only did he grow to like it, wine came to define who he was.

Claire Mawisa: What surprised you about the wine in particular, that there is more to understand in that world of wine?

Joseph Dhafana: Wine is a language. I take it as a language. It is a universal language.

V/O It was a language Joseph wanted to learn. He studied wine and all its complexities and set out on a mammoth expedition to learn from the experts.

Joseph Dhafana: In 2014 I drove 10 000 km in less than 3 months. I think just visiting vineyards. So that also helped me to polish my pallet.

V/O It was time well spent. He was told by those in the know that his palette was one of the best in the country. And in the world of wine connoisseurs that’s a crucial attribute.

Claire Mawisa: Mind blowing, because a sophisticated palette is a rare skill.

Joseph Dhafana: The talent might be there. It is like a game of football. You might be the best in the world but if you don’t practice you cannot have matched fitness.

V/O Meanwhile, Tinashe was building a reputation as a wine connoisseur himself. Not satisfied with just being a waiter who knew his grapes, he dreamt of being an expert - a sommelier - in a fine dining restaurant. Like Joseph, it would require a complex palette, the ability to appreciate wine on a completely different level.

Claire Mawisa: At what point do you realise that “my palette” is quite sophisticated”?

Tinashe Nyamudoka: That’s a progression. I think wine is about passion and how you explain it, how you understand it, how you decipher it to someone who really doesn’t understand wine and I think that was my greatest gift. I am a good wine communicator.

V/O Tinashe was now learning from some of the country’s best chefs, like the Test Kitchen’s Luke Dale Roberts, pairing individual dishes with different wines to enhance the flavour of both.

Luke Dale Roberts: Owner The Test Kitchen: I met him and my first impression was this guy is a gentle character, he is humble but more than that, he is passionate about wine. We have done everything from like taste wines together, share experiences. So we worked in tandem and it is always like such a pleasure.

Up sound

Tinashe Nyamudoka: I could come up with wine and food combinations and at some time he was like Tinashe this is really thought provoking and it made a whole difference in the Test Kitchen.

Link: The challenge Tinashe faced when studying wine was associating it with European fruits like black currents and quince that had little connection to the fruit and herbs he grew up with in his home country, Zimbabwe.

V/O Understanding wine on this level means recognising the characteristics it inherits from the very soil in which the vines grow. It’s a rare skill.

Tinashe Nyamudoka: For me when I smelt wine it took me back home like all those local indigenous fruits, mazhanje, maroro that I grew up eating and I could pick up in wine. That is how you associate wine so wine is about association.

V/O Their love of wine would bring Tinashe and Joseph together, two Zimbabweans united by a shared history as refugees. Their destination forever changed by the small bunches of fruit growing on vines on the farmlands of their new home. In 2017 they joined two of their countrymen in becoming the first all-black team of Zimbabweans to compete in the World Blind Wine Tasting Competition. Joseph was captain.

Up sound - Joseph and Claire in wine testing room
Subtitles: There is a time that I just wanted to taste… like sweat donkey, you know.
What!
Like cow dung. I pick all those things you know. Mainly red wine.

V/O: A sweaty donkey might not be the bouquet most of us expect from our wine, but it’s a level of appreciation you’d expect from someone now making his own.

Claire Mawisa: At what point did you realise or think you could produce your own wine?

Joseph Dhafana: I believe that we have different talents. So I just thought the best way of telling my story is through a bottle of wine. My story is bottled in that bottle of Mosi.

Up sound (Tinashe at table serving his own wine)

V/O Tinashe, like Joseph, wanted to create his own brand of wine.

Tinashe Nyamudoka: I wanted a wine brand that would express my Africanness, my culture.

V/O And so he called it ‘Kumusha’ meaning home, roots. And there’s additional symbolism for Tinashe who’s past roots are now firmly intertwined with those of the present in his new home, South Africa.

Tinashe Nyamudoka: I want to believe that now I am contributing to the larger economy because when I export my wine it’s not Zimbabwean wine, it is brand South africa.

V/O Joseph’s journey, despite all he’s achieved, remains incomplete.

Joseph: Apart from knowing Joseph as a sommelier, as a winemaker, I am huge in giving back to the community. I don’t think I am halfway through of where I want to be. I really feel I should found a foundation whereby I can be able to assist the little Josephs.
__________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________


PROMO ONE: 21 seconds
V/O How did two refugees fleeing from Zimbabwe’s economic crisis end up as top sommeliers in South Africa and making their own wine when they had no previous experience of wine?
Joseph Dhafana: I remember vividly that in 2014 I drove 10 000 km in less than 3 months. I think just visiting vineyards. So that also helped me to polish my pallet.

PROMO TWO: 21 seconds
V/O In a story of courage and hope we follow two Zimbabwean refugees on their journey through the vineyards to becoming top sommeliers and wine makers in a country they have embraced.
Tinashe Nyamudoka: I want to believe that now I am contributing to the larger economy because when I export my wine it’s not zimbabwean wine it is brand South africa.

PROMO THREE: 11 seconds
V/O They escaped poverty in Zimbabwe in search of a better future but what they found was a rare talent for wine that put them on the map as South Africa’s top sommeliers.

It’s also a story about two refugees. About desperation, perseverance and - ultimately - triumph. To tell it, we must start in Zimbabwe. Music up - change of pace V/O In 2009 Zimbabwe was on the brink: political turmoil and economic hardship saw anger spilling into the streets with a predictable and ofen ruthless response from the government. Hunger was widespread. Joseph Dhafana: Sommelier and wine maker: It was quite clear to all that that short period of time Zim was going through a crisis in terms of there was no food on the shelves. So there came really a time whereby I realise it is really pointless to be stuck in Zim. V/O Then 28 and working at a cement factory, Joseph Dhafana faced a stark choice: live with growing uncertainty or flee. Like thousands of others, he crossed into South Africa with just the clothes on his back. Joseph Dhafana: So I arrived in Musina and then I went straight to the refugee camp. Then I stayed there for almost two weeks until I was granted asylum which was to work and study in South Africa. Claire Mawisa: When you came to SA did you have a plan, did you have a job? Joseph Dhafana: I came down to Joburg and I lived in a Methodist church. So that time ladies could sleep in the church and gents in the streets. So I slept in the city of Joburg for about two weeks. Claire Mawisa: Where were you getting food? From bins, handouts? Joseph Dhafana: Foodwise I could actually get food from the streets and I could wait until I am super hungry then I would just eat without even looking what was on my plate. V/O It’s a struggle Tinashe Nyamudoka knows too well. Like Joseph, he had a job but chose to leave when he saw the writing on the wall. Tinashe Nyamudoka: Sommelier and wine maker: I was working in a supermarket, I was actually a junior manager and I saw first hand how the shelves were empty you know. You had money but you didn’t have anything to buy with it. V/O Tinashe made his way to Cape Town where he hoped to work in a supermarket. Tinashe Nyamudoka: Obviously you realise you don’t have the documentation required, second of all there weren’t positions for black people like me in those supermarkets so that was a bit of a reality check that sometimes the grass seems greener across but it was really tough. V/O He eventually got a job in a bakery and then in a restaurant. Claire Mawisa: So you say you got into restaurants. What were you doing in your first restaurant gig here in South Africa? Tinashe Nyamudoka: I just got employed because they were looking for inexperienced people. V/O Joseph’s search for work was more difficult. After weeks on Joh’burg’s streets he made his way to the Western Cape, settling in the wineland’s town of Riebeek Kasteel, where he lived in this shack. It was a move that would dramatically change his fortunes. Link: This is where Joseph first started working in Riebeek Kasteel as a gardener on this property but it didn’t take him long to move to a restaurant where he first worked as a barman, then a waiter. Joseph Dhafana: Now you have to understand Joseph is a rural boy, Joseph doesn’t even know a single easy cocktail. I don’t come from a background where wine was made. Wine wasn’t a thing. V/O His parents were strict Pentacostal Christians who frowned on alcohol. As a 29-year-old Joseph was to have his first taste. Joseph Dhafana: So 2010, still as a barman that is where I tried my very first sip of wine. Claire Mawisa; and how was it? Joseph Dhafana: And I didn’t like it. Claire Mawisa: (laughs) Joseph Dhafana: (smiles) V/O But not only did he grow to like it, wine came to define who he was. Claire Mawisa: What surprised you about the wine in particular, that there is more to understand in that world of wine? Joseph Dhafana: Wine is a language. I take it as a language. It is a universal language. V/O It was a language Joseph wanted to learn. He studied wine and all its complexities and set out on a mammoth expedition to learn from the experts. Joseph Dhafana: In 2014 I drove 10 000 km in less than 3 months. I think just visiting vineyards. So that also helped me to polish my pallet. V/O It was time well spent. He was told by those in the know that his palette was one of the best in the country. And in the world of wine connoisseurs that’s a crucial attribute. Claire Mawisa: Mind blowing, because a sophisticated palette is a rare skill. Joseph Dhafana: The talent might be there. It is like a game of football. You might be the best in the world but if you don’t practice you cannot have matched fitness. V/O Meanwhile, Tinashe was building a reputation as a wine connoisseur himself. Not satisfied with just being a waiter who knew his grapes, he dreamt of being an expert - a sommelier - in a fine dining restaurant. Like Joseph, it would require a complex palette, the ability to appreciate wine on a completely different level. Claire Mawisa: At what point do you realise that “my palette” is quite sophisticated”? Tinashe Nyamudoka: That’s a progression. I think wine is about passion and how you explain it, how you understand it, how you decipher it to someone who really doesn’t understand wine and I think that was my greatest gift. I am a good wine communicator. V/O Tinashe was now learning from some of the country’s best chefs, like the Test Kitchen’s Luke Dale Roberts, pairing individual dishes with different wines to enhance the flavour of both. Luke Dale Roberts: Owner The Test Kitchen: I met him and my first impression was this guy is a gentle character, he is humble but more than that, he is passionate about wine. We have done everything from like taste wines together, share experiences. So we worked in tandem and it is always like such a pleasure. Up sound Tinashe Nyamudoka: I could come up with wine and food combinations and at some time he was like Tinashe this is really thought provoking and it made a whole difference in the Test Kitchen. Link: The challenge Tinashe faced when studying wine was associating it with European fruits like black currents and quince that had little connection to the fruit and herbs he grew up with in his home country, Zimbabwe. V/O Understanding wine on this level means recognising the characteristics it inherits from the very soil in which the vines grow. It’s a rare skill. Tinashe Nyamudoka: For me when I smelt wine it took me back home like all those local indigenous fruits, mazhanje, maroro that I grew up eating and I could pick up in wine. That is how you associate wine so wine is about association. V/O Their love of wine would bring Tinashe and Joseph together, two Zimbabweans united by a shared history as refugees. Their destination forever changed by the small bunches of fruit growing on vines on the farmlands of their new home. In 2017 they joined two of their countrymen in becoming the first all-black team of Zimbabweans to compete in the World Blind Wine Tasting Competition. Joseph was captain. Up sound - Joseph and Claire in wine testing room Subtitles: There is a time that I just wanted to taste… like sweat donkey, you know. What! Like cow dung. I pick all those things you know. Mainly red wine. V/O: A sweaty donkey might not be the bouquet most of us expect from our wine, but it’s a level of appreciation you’d expect from someone now making his own. Claire Mawisa: At what point did you realise or think you could produce your own wine? Joseph Dhafana: I believe that we have different talents. So I just thought the best way of telling my story is through a bottle of wine. My story is bottled in that bottle of Mosi. Up sound (Tinashe at table serving his own wine) V/O Tinashe, like Joseph, wanted to create his own brand of wine. Tinashe Nyamudoka: I wanted a wine brand that would express my Africanness, my culture. V/O And so he called it ‘Kumusha’ meaning home, roots. And there’s additional symbolism for Tinashe who’s past roots are now firmly intertwined with those of the present in his new home, South Africa. Tinashe Nyamudoka: I want to believe that now I am contributing to the larger economy because when I export my wine it’s not Zimbabwean wine, it is brand South africa. V/O Joseph’s journey, despite all he’s achieved, remains incomplete. Joseph: Apart from knowing Joseph as a sommelier, as a winemaker, I am huge in giving back to the community. I don’t think I am halfway through of where I want to be. I really feel I should found a foundation whereby I can be able to assist the little Josephs. __________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ PROMO ONE: 21 seconds V/O How did two refugees fleeing from Zimbabwe’s economic crisis end up as top sommeliers in South Africa and making their own wine when they had no previous experience of wine? Joseph Dhafana: I remember vividly that in 2014 I drove 10 000 km in less than 3 months. I think just visiting vineyards. So that also helped me to polish my pallet. PROMO TWO: 21 seconds V/O In a story of courage and hope we follow two Zimbabwean refugees on their journey through the vineyards to becoming top sommeliers and wine makers in a country they have embraced. Tinashe Nyamudoka: I want to believe that now I am contributing to the larger economy because when I export my wine it’s not zimbabwean wine it is brand South africa. PROMO THREE: 11 seconds V/O They escaped poverty in Zimbabwe in search of a better future but what they found was a rare talent for wine that put them on the map as South Africa’s top sommeliers. ___________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for From refugees to sommeliers and wine makers (6125) Annalise Lubbe 11 April 2022

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): They arrived from Zimbabwe as refugees, in search of a better life, but their journey took them on an unexpected road of discovery and a taste of wine that put them on the map.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: This is a story of two non-drinkers from Zimbabwe ending up as award winning sommeliers and wine makers in the Cape after fleeing the country during economic meltdown 14 years ago. Tinashe Nyamudoka and Joseph Dhafana have worked their way up from menial jobs to earn a living and today they are respected sommeliers who have taken their passion for wine to the next level of wine producing their own brand.
metadata.Summary: In 2007 economic hardships hit Zimbabwe. Prices were doubling every 24 hours and a monthly wage would not even cover your bus fare. By 2008 roughly 1.5 million Zimbabwens were in South Africa. Among the growing numbers of Zimbabweans were Joseph Dhafana and Tinashe Nyamudoka who escaped poverty in search of a better life. Along their perilous journey they discovered a taste for wine which changed their lives from impoverished refugees to becoming leading sommeliers in the Western Cape and entering the global arena of wine tasting. Ten years after arriving in South Africa Dhafana and Nyamudoka, competed in the World Blind Wine Tasting Championship in Burgundy, France where some of the world’s top wines have to be identified in a blind tasting. Despite very little experience of international and local wines they came in 14th position in 2018 when they competed again. But their story did not end there. Since then they both tried their hand at wine making and took their brand to the international market: Nyamudoka with Mosi wines and Dhafana with Kumusha wines. Our story will track their stories and the exceptional talent they have for wine and what it took to succeed.
metadata.Further information: Joseph Dhafana: Joseph Dhafana and his wife Amelia arrived in South Africa in 2009. Despite many challenges including refugee camps and living in a Methodist Church in Johannesburg whilst awaiting asylum, they finally boarded a train from Johannesburg to Cape Town and found themselves in Riebeek Kasteel where Joseph started working as a gardener. Joseph joined Bar Bar Black Sheep restaurant as a dish washer and worked his way up through the kitchen, into the bar and onto the floor as a waiter. On his 29th birthday he tasted his first glass of wine, a Pieter Cruythoff Methode Cap Classique. Joseph remembered his initial sip of wine way back then was a bitter, acidic burn taste but was soon converted. Joseph recalls that with his mind in the vineyards, he pondered how someone could convert grapes to such a wonderful liquid. The wine bug followed him from that day. In 2013 Joseph enrolled at the Cape Wine Academy. He eventually left Riebeek Kasteel to further pursue his new-found passion in Cape Town and in 2014 got his first opportunity to produce his own wine at Antebellum Wines based at Meerhof Cellars. His meteoric rise to one of the most recognisable young figures in the wine industry is nothing short of remarkable. He worked at the internationally acclaimed La Colombe restaurant in Constantia as head sommelier, became a board member of the Black Cellar Club and was selected to represent South Africa in the World Blind Wine Tasting Championship in Burgundy in 2016 and the following two years as Zim team leader. In 2019 he left La Colombe to focus on his own wine label, Mosi wines and spirits, a tribute to his Zimbabwean origins and his family. Victoria Falls, known locally as Mosi-oa-tunya, are the face of the Mosi wine label. Joseph currently produces Tinashe Chenin Blanc which was named after his son and flavian Syrah, named after his dad who passed on in 2004. Joseph also produces gin and hopes to add Vodka to the mix in the near future. Tinashe Nyamudoka In 2009 Zimbabwe was going into an economic meltdown. At the time Tinash Myamudoka worked at a supermarket and experienced first-hand empty shelves. This prompted his move to South Africa where he found work polishing cutlery at a fine dining restaurant, The Roundhouse. After being promoted to waiter and without any prior experience of wine, Tinash learned from the beverage director, eventually landina job as a wine steward at Nobu - an establishment of the One & Only group. In 2013 he won the Reaching for the Young Stars Best wine Steward Award. He then worked at the Oyster Box hotel in Durban, before returning to Cape Town to become the head sommelier at The Test Kitchen. Under the guidance of award winning chef and owner of the restaurant Tinashe hones his skills at one of the world’s top 50 best restaurants under the guidance of Dale Luke Robert, head chef and owner. He wins the Eat Out Wine Service Award and with a head for business he completed his diploma from the Cape Wine academy, a Certificate from the Court Master Sommeliers Europe, A certificate in Wine Business Management from the University of Cape Town’s Graduate School of Business and a Michael Fridjhon Wine Judging Academy certificate. By now Tinashe had extended his wine tasting experience as a top sommelier and felt the time was ripe to try his hand at winemaking. With his roots still firmly entrenched in Zimbabwe he called his brand, Kumusha, meaning ‘your roots’, ‘your home’, ‘your origin’. The challenge he faced when studying wines was associating it with European fruits such as black currents and quince. He always yearned to connect it to indigenous flavours and aromas that resonated with on and ther spaces,hence Kumusha Wines flavours are wild fruits he grew up eating at home. For example, he used the leaf of a black jack (‘Knapse Kerels') - a typical weed that sticks to your clothes - to replace the traditional Black Currant leaf flavour. In 2020 Tinashe leaves his position as sommelier at the Test Kitchen to focus entirely on Kumusha wines which are now exported to USA, Zimbabwe, Kenya and the Netherlands and can now add the UK after a recent visit to break into this difficult market. Fast forward to March 2022 and Tinashe is back at the Test Kitchen! This time a brand new restaurant in Johannesburg where Dale Luke Roberts have designed the ultimate culinary experience in a 12 course menu complimented by a carefully selected wine list put together by Tinashe. Ask what the future holds for Tinashe and he already has his eyes set on making his own brandy to add to his wine making skills and hope to one day go grow wine on his grandfather’s farm in Zimbabwe. The story: Our story starts in a very busy Test Kitchen restaurant where the action and pace is fast. Tinashe goes through the wine selection, the chef prepares designer meals and the clock is ticking. From here we will go back to the past of where Tinashe started when he came to South Africa as a migrant and ending up as a top sommelier and wine maker. Joseph’s story will be captured at the tin shack where he lived for a while in Riebeek Kasteel when he was working as a gardner at the Bar Bar Black Sheep restaurant in Riebeek Kasteel up to his winemaking at the local co-op where Mosi wines are bottled. Interviews will be with Joseph and Tinashe and a short interview with Dale Luke Roberts who can talk about the importance of wine pairing and having a top sommelier on your dining room floor. __________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
